halbach_optimization._design: Two rings under a hard budget of fewer than 12 magnets: 10 cubes of 24 mm N52, four rings of 2 and 3, 58 mm long over the end cubes and 210 mm across, with a 70 mm free bore. As run it gives 84 mT - 3.57 MHz for protons - and 9396 ppm over a 4 mm sample sphere. That is nearly one percent, and it is not a working NMR magnet. It is here because the constraint was asked for, and this is what the constraint costs.
halbach_optimization._the_constraint: Two ring positions times two layers is four rings, so the total is 4N + 2d for an inner count N and an outer offset d. Every combination under 12 needs N of 1 or 2, and a ring of fewer than three magnets is not a Halbach ring: the identities that leave a uniform field, sum(cos 2t) = 0 and sum(cos^2 t) = N/2, first hold at N = 3. The smallest genuine two ring Halbach here is N = 3 with d = 0, which is exactly 12 magnets and so just outside the budget. N = 2 with d = 1, ten magnets in rings of 2, 3, 2, 3, is the most the budget allows and the best allocation in it, since the outer rings at least reach three. The inner pair does not, and that is why the numbers below are what they are.
halbach_optimization._ring_separation: 34 mm. It barely matters. With no uniform term to work with, the optimizer's only strategy is to move everything away from the sample, and it rails at whatever radius the candidate list allows however the separation is set: with the list reaching 52 mm it returns 52 mm, with the list reaching 72 mm it returns 72 mm and still 6800 ppm at a 250 mm outside diameter. There is no interior optimum. The list is capped at 52 mm here to keep the magnet a sane size rather than to find a minimum, because there is not one to find.
halbach_optimization._element: 24 mm N52 cubes, the largest in this family, because with two magnets to a ring nothing else gives any field at all. A 24 mm N52 cube weighs about 100 g and the force between two in contact runs to hundreds of newtons. Handle with jigs and gloves.
halbach_optimization._candidates: 31 radii from 22 to 52 mm, every one carrying two magnets - the count is set by the budget, not by packing, and two cubes on a ring are never close to touching. With one gene this list is the entire search space, and the answer is simply its top entry.
halbach_optimization._layers: 36 mm out with one more magnet, the closest two layers of 24 mm cubes can sit. The outer rings are the only real Halbach rings in this magnet, and they are the far ones.
halbach_optimization._symmetry: full rather than octant. A ring of two or three magnets carries a low order harmonic that the octant reflections do not respect, so an eighth of the sphere is not a fair sample of the field. See the same note in the three ring version, where the difference between the two was 531 ppm against an honest 719.
halbach_optimization._dsv: 4 mm, a capillary. Asking for more only makes the number larger.
halbach_optimization._genetic: One gene over 31 radii. Crossover is inert on a one gene genome and the population sees every candidate in generation zero, so this is an exhaustive scan and the settings say so rather than search.
halbach_optimization._verdict: Do not build this. 9396 ppm is a field varying by nearly one percent across a 4 mm sample: at 3.57 MHz the line would be some 34 kHz wide, and no FID worth acquiring survives it. It also needs a 210 mm outside diameter and 100 g magnets to achieve that. The constraint of fewer than twelve magnets sits below the floor where a two layer Halbach exists at all, and the honest answer to the request is this number rather than a design. If the count is what matters, three_ring_21magnets_halbach_optim.json does 602 ppm with 21 magnets; if the magnet matters, two_ring_halbach_optim.json does 246 ppm with 86.
